title: The fifteen-minute weekly review: look back to move forward
description: Once a week, for fifteen minutes, ask three questions: what went well, what was hard, and what is the one thing next week needs? A tiny review that keeps a busy life steerable.
author: SparkKindly · AI-assisted

body.heading: Three questions, in order
paragraphs: Start with what went well — and be specific. “Tuesday's walk before work” teaches you more than “a good week”. Wins recorded weekly become evidence you can use on the days when everything feels stalled.

Then what was hard, without turning it into a trial. You are a reporter, not a judge: note what drained time, what surprised you, and what you kept postponing. Postponed three weeks running is information, not failure — the task may be too big, too vague, or simply not wanted.

body.heading: End with one thing
paragraphs: Close by choosing the single most useful focus for next week and writing it where you will see it. One focus, visibly chosen, beats a list of nine intentions that quietly expire by Wednesday.

Fifteen minutes is the whole design. A review short enough to survive your busiest week will still be running in six months, and six months of small corrections will steer you further than one grand annual overhaul.

body.heading: Make it a fixture
paragraphs: Attach the review to something that already happens weekly — Sunday tea, the Friday train, the last work call. Same time, same notebook, same three questions.
Over time the notebook becomes a map of your year written by the only person who was actually there. Few planning tools can say that, and none of them cost fifteen minutes.

takeaway: Fifteen minutes, three questions, one focus for next week: a review small enough to keep is powerful enough to steer by.
